title: The Thank-You Email After an Interview (and Exactly When to Follow Up)
summary: Send the thank-you email within 24 hours, then follow up on a schedule: wait past a stated decision date, or about a week, then one more nudge, then let go.
body_text: When should you send a thank-you email and follow up after an interview? Get a short, specific thank-you email out within about 24 hours, same day or the next morning. Then you wait. Did they name a decision date? Hold until a business day past it. No date given? Give it roughly a week, then one polite follow-up. Still silence after another week or so, send one more and let it go. The email almost never wins the job on its own. It's a cheap signal of interest though, and it happens to be the one thing you actually control once you've walked out of the room. Here's the honest version nobody puts in a listicle. The thank-you email is not magic. It won't rescue a bad interview, it can't out-argue a candidate the panel liked more, and by the time it lands the decision is usually already forming. Debriefs often happen minutes after you leave, while the interviewers still remember your handshake. So if the interview itself went sideways, a note won't undo it, and your energy is better spent recovering from a rough interview in other ways. And yet. A hiring manager sitting on two candidates she genuinely can't separate will take any tiebreaker she can get. A note that lands the same afternoon, references something real from the conversation, and sounds like a person wrote it can nudge that. A generic one BCC'd to four people can quietly cost you. So the smart move isn't to obsess over the email or to skip it out of spite. It's to send a good one fast, then run a follow-up schedule that reads as interested instead of frantic. This piece is about the timing. When the thank-you goes out, how long you wait before the first nudge, when the second nudge is fair game, and the point where silence just means no. If you want the exact wording of a follow-up message, we point you to the step-by-step follow-up guide at the right spot. Everything here is the schedule underneath it. Does a thank-you email even matter in 2026? Ask ten hiring managers and you'll get a split you can practically hear. One camp treats the whole ritual as a relic. Veteran managers who've been hiring for decades will tell you a thank-you letter has never once given a candidate a leg up, because they already know by the time the interview ends. The candidate debrief tends to happen right after you leave, with the three or four people who were in the room, and the decision to move forward often gets locked in before anyone could have written a note. If you've ever wondered how hiring actually works behind the scenes , the speed of that debrief is exactly why the note has such a narrow window to matter. The other camp isn't sentimental about it either, but they'll call it a minor plus. The scenario where it earns its keep is a panel weighing two candidates it genuinely can't separate. One sends a thank-you, one doesn't, and a couple of people on the panel read that as follow-through, as someone who closes the loop. Would it rescue a weak candidate? No. But when the vote is a coin flip, you want every small thing pointing your way. Both camps are right, and that's the useful part. The note is a low-cost professionalism signal. It rarely moves a clear decision. It can tip a genuine tie. A small minority of interviewers will actually notice its absence and hold a faint mark against you, which is unfair but real, and cheap to insure against. There's an old data point people love to quote here: a 2017 Accountemps survey of more than 300 HR managers at US companies found 80% said they factor thank-you messages into the hiring call, while only about a quarter of candidates ever sent one. Treat that number as directional and dated, not gospel, because it's nearly a decade old and the market has churned since. The direction still holds. Most people who receive them notice; most candidates don't bother. So the calibrated answer is boring and correct. Send one. Keep it short. Don't expect it to carry you, and don't lose sleep if you forget once. The bigger lever is what you do over the next two weeks, not the email itself. When to send the thank-you: the 24-hour window Same day, or first thing the next morning. That's the window. Send it while you're still fresh in their memory and while the interview loop is still warm. The logic is simple. A note that arrives four days later reads like an afterthought, and by then they may have already moved. A note that fires off ninety seconds after you close your laptop can read a little manic. Somewhere in the middle, that evening or the next breakfast, is the sweet spot where it feels considered rather than either forgotten or frantic. There's a quieter reason the same-day note helps. Some interviewers don't finalize their written assessment right when you leave. On a one-on-one they'll sit down at the end of the day and write you up, and a thoughtful note that landed in the meantime is sitting right there in the inbox as they do it. You can't count on that, and plenty of teams have already decided, but it costs you nothing to have your email be the last thing they read before they type their notes. This matters more when the process is a marathon of stages, and if you're wondering why there are so many interview rounds now, each round is another chance for a clean note to keep you memorable. One practical wrinkle. If you didn't get anyone's email address, don't play detective and guess it, which reads as creepy. Reply up the chain instead. Send the note to the recruiter or coordinator who scheduled you and ask them to pass it along. They do this all the time, and routing it through them is perfectly normal. What to actually write (and what makes it worse) Short. Specific. Human. Three words, and most people miss at least one. Short means four or five sentences, not a second cover letter. Specific means you name something real from the conversation, the roadmap detail they mentioned, the problem the team is chewing on, the offhand thing you both got animated about. That single specific is what separates a note that lands from a note that reads like a template pulled off the internet, which every recruiter can smell instantly. Human means it sounds like you talking, not a business-letter cosplay. The core moves inside it: Thank them for their time, once, and move on. You already said it in the room. This is the written echo, not a grovel. Reaffirm your interest in the role, concretely. "I left even more interested in the platform team's roadmap" beats "I am very excited about this opportunity." Optionally, add one thing. If a question caught you flat and you thought of a better answer on the drive home, this is your one clean shot to add it. If you're worried you undersold a specific skill, a sentence fixes it. One point, not five. Now the ways people torpedo it. The over-the-top grovel, gushing about how fascinated you've always been by the company's internal systems, reads as desperate and a little insincere. Re-selling your entire resume in bullet form misses the point. A typo, especially in the name of the person or the company, quietly undoes the whole "detail-oriented" impression you're trying to build. And the classic panel mistake, which comes next. Keep it clean and it does its small job. Overthink it and you turn a free plus into a liability. Panel interviews: send individual notes, not one blast If you met three people, send three notes. Not one email with everyone in the To line, and definitely not one identical message copy-pasted and fired at each address in sequence. Why it matters: panels compare. They sit in a room afterward and talk about you, and if two of them mention "she sent a nice note" and pull up word-for-word the same paragraph, the effect flips from thoughtful to lazy. The whole value of the note is that it feels personal, and nothing kills that faster than the reveal that it was a mail merge. You don't need to write four essays. Keep the same warm skeleton, then swap the specific in each one. The engineering lead talked you through the migration, so that note references the migration. The manager dug into how you handle conflict, so that note picks up the thread you started. It takes ten extra minutes and it's the difference between "he closed the loop" and "he thanked us all with the same paragraph." No addresses for the panel? Same fix as before. One note to the recruiter, ask them to forward it around, and mention you'd have written to each individually if you'd had their emails. That's honest and it still lands as polite. A thank-you note can't fix an interview that went sideways. Practice the answers first so the conversation is actually worth following up on, then send the note from a position of strength. Prep with Hiration Interview Prep → The follow-up timeline: exactly when to nudge Here's the schedule most people get wrong, usually by nudging way too soon and then way too often. The thank-you and the follow-up are two different things. The thank-you is courtesy, sent right away. The follow-up is a status check, and its timing depends entirely on one question: did they tell you when they'd get back to you? Step one, within 24 hours: the thank-you. Covered above. This is not a follow-up. Don't ask for a status update in it, that's premature and it muddies a note that should just be gracious. Step two: figure out your clock. The single best thing you can do to avoid the whole "when do I follow up" spiral is to ask in the interview. One of your closing questions should be some version of "What do the next steps look like, and when do you expect to make a decision?" Their answer sets your timeline. If they say "by end of next week," you now know exactly when the ball is in your court. This is also the cheapest way to look composed instead of anxious, and it's covered in more depth in our guide on the questions to ask your interviewer . Step three, if they gave you a date: wait until that date passes, then give it one business day, then follow up. Not the morning of. Not the day before because you're anxious. Hiring runs late constantly, someone's out, the panel can't get on a call, the approval is stuck two levels up. Giving them a business-day cushion past their own deadline shows you were listening and you're not going to hound them the second the clock ticks over. Part of why they set a date and then blow through it is mundane: they're waiting to see if their first choice accepts before they close the loop with anyone else. Your patience past the deadline is you giving that process room to breathe. Step three, if they gave you no date: wait about five to seven business days, call it a week, before the first nudge. A week is long enough that you're not pouncing and short enough that the role is probably still live. Fire off a follow-up two days after the interview with no deadline in play and you're the person who "follows up too quickly," which lands on more than one hiring manager's quiet list of turn-offs, right next to showing up forty minutes early. That first follow-up itself is short: reaffirm your interest, ask politely where things stand, offer anything else they need. For the exact phrasing and a template you can adapt, use the dedicated how-to-follow-up guide . The wording is the easy part once the clock is right; it's the timing people botch. The second follow-up, and when to stop Say your first nudge gets you nothing. Not a rejection, not an update, just quiet. You get one more. Wait roughly another week, then send a second, even shorter follow-up. Reaffirm interest one last time, keep it warm, no guilt-tripping, no "I haven't heard back and I'm confused." Something like a brief note that you're still very interested and wanted to check whether there's any update, and you understand these things take time. That's the ceiling. Two follow-ups, spaced about a week apart, after the thank-you. Picture over-persistence from their side. Here's a slow-motion version people go through: given a callback date, wait ten business days past it, follow up, get told holidays caused delays, wait two more weeks, follow up again, get told things are being finalized. Seven weeks in, the answer lands as an automated form rejection. The lesson isn't that following up failed. It's that no number of emails was going to change an answer that had probably been settled for a month, just add to your own frustration. So the discipline is this. Never daily. Never five emails. Never the same week twice. Space them out, keep each one short and warm, and cap it at two. Anything past that stops reading as interest and starts reading as a warning sign, the same category of desperation signal that makes employers nervous. The candidate who checks in twice, calmly, over three weeks looks like someone who wants the job. The candidate who emails every other day looks like someone who's going to be hard to manage. When silence just means no At some point you have to call it. After two unanswered follow-ups spread across two or three weeks, the humane thing to do for yourself is to treat it as a no and mentally move on. Not with bitterness, just with realism. They know you're waiting. If they wanted you, the wait itself would feel different, and you'd know. Moving on doesn't mean burning the bridge. Leave the door cracked. If they resurface in a month with an offer or a "sorry for the delay, are you still available," that's a pleasant surprise, and you handle it graciously. But you don't hold your job search hostage to a company that's gone dark. You keep applying, keep interviewing, keep your pipeline full, and you let this one drift into the background where a stalled process belongs. Here's the part that actually matters for your sanity. The silence is almost never about you. Ghosting after interviews is rampant, and it's a story about broken hiring processes far more than it's a verdict on your candidacy. Reqs get frozen, budgets vanish, the role gets quietly restructured, or the internal candidate you never knew about gets the nod. Recruiters themselves admit the follow-through on their side is often a mess. If you've internalized the reality of the post-application black hole , none of this should surprise you. A great thank-you email and a disciplined follow-up cadence cannot fix a process that was never going to close. What they can do is keep you top of mind for the roles that are still moving. That's the whole trade. You do the small professional things well, you accept you can't control the rest, and you spend your real energy on the next interview. Reading the signals (carefully) People desperately want the thank-you and follow-up window to be a decoder ring for whether they got the job. Be careful here. Most of the tea leaves are noise. A reply to your thank-you is a mild positive. It usually means someone with authority read it and felt like responding, and top candidates do tend to get warmer, faster replies because the team wants to keep them engaged. But plenty of companies have a blanket "don't respond to candidate emails" policy, so no reply means very little on its own. Some candidates swear they can read the shift, quick 24-hour replies to earlier notes and then sudden silence on the latest one, as a tell that they've been passed over. Maybe. Treat that as a gut feeling, not a fact. It's the kind of pattern that's right often enough to feel true and wrong often enough to burn you. The cleaner signals live elsewhere in the process. Being asked about your timeline and competing offers, meeting more of the team, a recruiter who suddenly wants your references or salary expectations, those move the needle far more than whether someone hit reply on your thank-you note. If you want the fuller list, we've written up the signs you're likely to get the job . The short version: don't build a mood around an email response. Build it around whether the process keeps pulling you forward. The 2026 reality: the one lever you control The market right now is brutal on the follow-up front. People apply into voids, interview into silence, and get automated rejections weeks later, if they get anything at all. It's easy to conclude the whole ritual is pointless. It isn't, but its purpose has narrowed. Here's the reframe. You can't make a frozen req thaw. You can't force a ghosting company to close its loop. You can't out-email a decision that's already made. What you can do is be the candidate who was fast, specific, gracious, and appropriately patient, so that for every role still genuinely in motion, you're the one who left a clean, professional impression and stayed warm without being a pest. In a pile where half the field either sends a template or sends nothing, that's a real edge. Small, but real, and free. And the biggest lever of all sits upstream of any of this. The follow-up can only carry an interview that actually went well, so the highest-return move is walking into the room ready. Rehearse your answers out loud, tighten your stories, and get comfortable on camera before the virtual interview or the panel. Hiration's Interview Prep gives you that practice, and a ChatGPT mock interview is a decent free warm-up too. A strong interview plus a clean, well-timed follow-up is the whole formula. The note alone was never going to do it. A quick note on format, since it comes up. Email is the default. A mailed handwritten card, once the gold standard, now often reads as slightly out of touch and arrives too late to matter for a fast-moving decision anyway. Send the email. If the culture is unusually traditional and the timeline is slow, a card can be a nice second touch, but it's the exception. And if you're running a heavy search, twenty or thirty conversations across a couple of weeks, give yourself grace. The risk of a rushed note with the wrong name in it climbs fast when you're that stretched. Better to send four good notes than fourteen sloppy ones. Do the roles you actually want properly, and don't let a follow-up spreadsheet become its own second job. The short list of what not to do Because it's easier to name the traps than to memorize the rules: Don't send a template. A recruiter clocks a copy-pasted note in seconds, and it does less than nothing. Don't grovel or re-pitch your whole resume. The note is a handshake, not a closing argument. Don't blast one identical email to a panel. Individual notes, or nothing. Don't get the name or company wrong. That one typo undoes the whole detail-oriented impression. Don't follow up before you've given them their own stated timeline plus a business day, or about a week if they gave you nothing. Don't follow up more than twice. Two calm nudges, spaced out, is the cap. Don't read a non-reply as a rejection, and don't read a reply as an offer. Watch the process, not the inbox. Don't tie up your whole search waiting on one company. Keep applying while you wait. Do those, and you've handled the after-interview stretch about as well as it can be handled. The rest is out of your hands, which, honestly, is the most freeing thing to accept about the whole job search. You control the note, the timing, and your own composure. You don't control the answer. Send a good email, run a clean cadence, and go get the next interview. Frequently Asked Questions How long after an interview should I send a thank-you email? Within about 24 hours. Same day is ideal, the next morning is fine. Later than that and it reads as an afterthought, and the interview loop may have already moved on. Don't fire it off within minutes of leaving either, since that can look a little frantic. That evening or the following breakfast is the sweet spot. Do thank-you emails actually help you get the job? Rarely on their own. A note won't rescue a weak interview or beat a stronger candidate. Where it helps is a genuine tie, where an interviewer takes any small signal of interest and professionalism as a tiebreaker. A minority of interviewers also notice its absence. So it's a cheap plus, not a deciding factor. Send one, but don't expect it to carry you. How long should I wait before following up after an interview? Depends on whether they gave you a decision date. If they did, wait until that date passes, add one business day, then follow up. If they didn't, give it roughly a week, five to seven business days. Following up two days later with no deadline in play tends to read as too eager, which works against you. How many times can I follow up after an interview? Twice, after the thank-you. One nudge on your timeline, and if that's met with silence, one more about a week later, then you stop. Beyond that it stops signaling interest and starts signaling desperation. Space them out, keep each one short and warm, and never send them on consecutive days. They said they'd get back to me by Friday and it's now Monday. What do I do? Wait until Monday's business day is basically done, or nudge Tuesday morning, then send a short, friendly check-in reaffirming your interest and asking where things stand. Hiring runs late all the time, often because they're waiting on their first choice before closing with anyone else. A day or two past a stated date is normal, so keep the tone easy rather than accusatory. Should I send separate thank-you notes to a panel? Yes. Send each person their own. The mistake that backfires is one email with everyone CC'd, or worse, the identical paragraph pasted to all four addresses, because panels sit around afterward and compare, and a mail-merge gets exposed instantly. Keep the same warm skeleton, then swap in a detail that only came up in that person's part of the conversation. No addresses? Fire one note to the recruiter and ask them to pass it around. What should a thank-you email actually say? Four or five sentences, tops. Thank them once, say you left more interested and point to something concrete about the role, and drop in one specific from the actual conversation so it can't be mistaken for a template. If a question caught you off guard, this is your shot to add the answer you thought of afterward. Then stop. No grovel, no resume in bullet form, and please check the spelling of every name. What does it mean if they don't reply to my thank-you email? On its own, almost nothing. Loads of companies have a flat policy against responding to candidate emails, so quiet there is not a rejection. If you do get a warm, fast reply, take it as a mild good sign, since teams like to keep the people they want engaged. But you're reading the wrong tea leaf if you fixate on the inbox. Watch whether the process keeps pulling you forward instead: another round scheduled, references requested, questions about your timeline. How do I know when to stop following up and move on? Once two follow-ups over two or three weeks have gone unanswered, call it. Treat it as a no, and put your energy into the next opportunity. Leave the door cracked in case they resurface late, which happens more than you'd think, but never freeze your search for a company that went dark on you. Nine times out of ten the silence is their broken process rather than a verdict on you, so keep that pipeline moving. Is a handwritten thank-you note better than email in 2026? Usually not, and this surprises people. Email is what you send. A card in the mail used to be the classy move, but now it can read as a bit out of touch, and it lands days too late for any decision that's moving quickly. Get the email out inside 24 hours. If you're in an old-school field where things crawl, a card can be a nice extra touch on top, though it shouldn't be the whole play. title: Accelerating Grid Modernization for the Age of Electricity
summary: Explore how smart meters, battery energy storage, solid-state transformers and cybersecurity can modernize the grid for rising power demand.
body_text: Power Delivery at AI Scale: The Case for Solid-State Transformers Conventional power transformers have served the grid reliably for generations, stepping voltage up and down at key points across the network. But they do so passively, with limited ability to respond dynamically as load conditions shift. That model worked for a grid built around stable generation and predictable demand. It is far less suited to one now supporting data center demand that the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) estimates could account for up to 17% of U.S. electricity generation by 2030. Solid-state transformers (SSTs) represent a fundamentally different approach and are an ideal match for what the grid needs now. Rather than passively converting voltage, they use power electronics to actively manage power flow in real time, enabling dynamic voltage regulation, bidirectional energy flow, and tighter integration with storage and variable loads. As utilities incorporate more renewable generation into the grid, that flexibility becomes increasingly important for managing fluctuating power flows across the network. Their modular design allows them to scale to application requirements — from flexible substation configurations to high-density data center power delivery — while their compact footprint reduces installation costs and site requirements compared to conventional units. For grid operators and developers contending with aging infrastructure and compressed build timelines, SSTs deliver the control and flexibility that conventional equipment cannot. The sourcing landscape for that conventional equipment makes the case for SSTs still more compelling. Supply concerns can appear overnight, particularly when the demand side of the equation is so dynamic, but SSTs are likely to face far fewer headwinds than the earlier generation Conventional Low-Frequency Transformers (LFTs), which have been the backbone of power distribution for over a century. The U.S. remains heavily dependent on imported LFTs due to limited domestic manufacturing capacity and the difficulty of sourcing specialized grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) . Lead times for large power transformers, which averaged roughly 50 weeks in the early 2020s, have now stretched to as long as two to four years . At the same time, however, demand is accelerating. Wood Mackenzie reports that power transformer demand has increased 119% since 2019 , with distribution transformer demand up 34%, driven by load growth, renewable integration, and a wave of end-of-life replacements. For grid operators and data center developers, those wait times represent a direct constraint on build schedules. SSTs’ shorter implementation timelines and reduced dependence on an import-constrained supply chain offer a practical path around it. Smarter infrastructure, however, brings an expanded attack surface. As the grid adds connected devices, from intelligent meters to BESS management systems to solid-state converters, each new node requires the same security disciplines applied to the hardware itself.

title: GLP-1 Telehealth Treatment for Teens — 100% Virtual Pediatric Care

body_text: According to the CDC, more than 1 in 5 U.S. adolescents now has obesity — a number that continues to rise. Childhood obesity is not just a number on a scale. It increases a teen's risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, fatty liver disease, sleep apnea, and joint problems. It can also take a serious toll on mental health, contributing to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem during an already challenging time. For families who have tried lifestyle changes without lasting results, GLP-1 telehealth for teens may be a safe, effective next step. Blueberry Balance makes it possible to access FDA-approved GLP-1 treatment online, led entirely by board-certified pediatricians , without leaving home. Why consider GLP-1 medications for teenagers? When severe obesity persists despite sustained efforts with diet, exercise, and behavioral changes, the health risks — from type 2 diabetes to cardiovascular disease — can accumulate quickly during adolescence. That is why the American Academy of Pediatrics now recommends considering pharmacotherapy as part of a comprehensive treatment approach for adolescents with obesity. Blueberry Balance is a comprehensive, 100% virtual weight management program designed specifically for adolescents ages 12 and older. Here is what you need to know about how it works, who qualifies, and what to expect. What Is Blueberry Balance? Blueberry Balance is a pediatrician-led telehealth program that provides virtual GLP-1 prescribing for adolescents struggling with obesity. Unlike adult-focused weight loss clinics, every aspect of Blueberry Balance is built around the unique medical, developmental, and emotional needs of adolescents. The program uses only FDA-approved, brand-name GLP-1 medications — compounded GLP-1s are not part of the program. Wegovy (semaglutide) is the only GLP-1 medication currently FDA-approved for weight management in adolescents ages 12 and older. Your teen's pediatrician will determine the best treatment plan based on their individual needs and current FDA approvals. Alongside medication, the program includes ongoing behavioral support, nutritional guidance, exercise counseling, and continuous medical monitoring. This comprehensive approach aligns with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline , which recommends pharmacotherapy alongside intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment for adolescents with obesity. How It Works Getting started with teen weight loss telehealth through Blueberry Balance is straightforward. The entire process happens virtually, so your teen never misses school for an appointment. Step 1: Online Consultation Your teen's journey begins with a comprehensive virtual consultation with a board-certified pediatrician. During this visit, the care team reviews your teen's medical history, current BMI, and overall health. They also conduct required screenings — including assessments for eating disorders, depression, and metabolic health — to ensure GLP-1 medication is appropriate and safe. Step 2: Personalized Treatment Plan If your teen qualifies, their pediatrician creates a personalized treatment plan that includes the right medication at the right dose, along with nutrition coaching and behavioral support. Because these medications require a careful dose escalation period — the timeline varies depending on the specific medication prescribed — your teen's plan includes frequent virtual check-ins to monitor progress and manage any side effects. Step 3: Ongoing Monitoring and Support Weight management is a long-term commitment, and Blueberry Balance provides continuous care throughout. Your teen receives regular telehealth visits, lab work reviews, growth monitoring, and mental health check-ins. Connected health devices like smart scales allow the care team to track progress between visits — all from the comfort of home. Ready to see if your teen qualifies? Join Blueberry Balance today. What’s Included Blueberry Balance provides everything your teen needs for safe, effective GLP-1 treatment: Virtual consultations with board-certified pediatricians experienced in adolescent obesity FDA-approved GLP-1 medication prescribing and ongoing dose management Guided dose escalation with frequent check-ins (timeline varies by medication) Nutritional counseling and behavioral health referrals Regular lab work coordination (done at a local lab, reviewed by your teen's care team) Growth and development monitoring tailored for adolescents Mental health screening at baseline and throughout treatment Secure messaging with your teen's care team between visits Coordination with your teen's primary care provider, including shared records, referral letters, and PCP notification View full pricing and plan details . Who Is Eligible? GLP-1 medications are FDA-approved for use in adolescents ages 12 and older. However, eligibility is highly individual — your teen's pediatrician will evaluate their specific health profile, medical history, and needs to determine whether GLP-1 treatment is appropriate for them. Certain conditions may prevent your teen from using GLP-1 medications, including a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN2). GLP-1 medications also carry FDA warnings for acute pancreatitis, acute gallbladder disease, hypoglycemia (particularly when combined with insulin secretagogues), and suicidal ideation or behavior. Your teen's pediatrician will review all eligibility criteria and safety considerations during the initial consultation, and will monitor for these risks throughout treatment. What to Expect: Common Side Effects GLP-1 medications are generally well-tolerated, but gastrointestinal side effects are common, particularly during dose escalation. In the STEP TEENS clinical trial, approximately 60% of adolescents taking semaglutide reported GI side effects, compared with about 36% on placebo. The most common side effects include: Nausea Vomiting Diarrhea Abdominal pain Constipation These side effects are typically mild to moderate and often improve as your teen's body adjusts to the medication. Your Blueberry Balance care team actively monitors for side effects at every check-in and adjusts the treatment plan as needed to keep your teen comfortable. Our Pediatric Team Every Blueberry Balance provider is a board-certified pediatrician with specialized training in adolescent medicine and obesity management. Your teen receives care from doctors who understand pediatric-specific FDA guidelines, dosing protocols, and the emotional challenges of weight management during adolescence. Frequently Asked Questions Can my teen get GLP-1 medication through telehealth? Yes. GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy) are not controlled substances, which means they are not subject to the federal controlled-substance telehealth restrictions that limit some other medications. Blueberry Balance pediatricians conduct thorough virtual evaluations and prescribe FDA-approved medications when clinically appropriate. Wegovy is approved for weight management in adolescents ages 12 and older. How does virtual prescribing work for weight loss medication? Your teen meets with a board-certified pediatrician via secure video. The doctor reviews medical history, conducts required screenings, and — if your teen qualifies — prescribes the appropriate GLP-1 medication. The prescription is sent to your pharmacy, and the care team follows up regularly to monitor progress, adjust dosing, and manage any side effects. Is telehealth as effective as in-person care for GLP-1 management? Telehealth is well-suited for GLP-1 management because the treatment requires frequent monitoring, especially during the dose escalation period. Virtual visits make it easier to schedule these regular check-ins without disrupting your teen's school schedule. Lab work is completed locally, and results are reviewed remotely by your teen's care team. Emerging evidence supports telehealth as a promising model for ongoing medication management and behavioral health support. What states is Blueberry Balance available in? Blueberry Balance is expanding availability. Contact us to confirm whether the program is available in your state. Ready to explore GLP-1 telehealth for your teen? Join Blueberry Balance today. Get Started Today Taking the first step toward your teen's health does not have to be complicated. With Blueberry Balance, your family gets access to board-certified pediatricians, FDA-approved GLP-1 treatment, and comprehensive support — all through a 100% virtual program built specifically for teens. title: Centralize human and agentic work with Datadog Work Management
summary: Learn how Datadog Work Management helps you coordinate human and AI agent–driven work while preserving context, ownership, and activity across tools.
body_text: Roxanne Moslehi Product Manager Teams often track operational work across spreadsheets, Slack threads, Jira tickets, and whatever system generated the original alert or signal. This fragmentation makes it difficult to maintain a consistent record of what needs attention, who or what is addressing the issue, and what has already happened. As AI agents take on more responsibility for investigations, triage, and code changes, the number of handoffs grows, making ownership, status, and history even harder to preserve. Datadog Work Management , formerly Case Management, provides a single place to track work created by humans, automations, and Datadog AI agents. Each work item includes relevant Datadog context, such as logs, traces, monitors, and service ownership, and tracks assignments, approvals, artifacts, and activity over time. Work Management integrates with Datadog products such as Cloud SIEM , Error Tracking , and Monitors , as well as external systems such as Slack, GitHub, and Jira. These integrations keep each work item up to date as people and Datadog AI agents contribute to it. In this post, we’ll explain how Work Management helps you: Track alerts from detection through resolution Turn feature requests into merged code Investigate and resolve security signals in Cloud SIEM Centralize work while preserving each team’s processes Track alerts from detection through resolution Work Management provides a continuous record of an alert from its initial trigger through investigation, escalation, and follow-up. For example, consider an SRE who is on call for an ecommerce service and receives a critical-priority alert about a large number of checkout errors. The alert automatically creates a work item that includes the relevant logs, traces, monitors, and service ownership, so the SRE starts with the necessary context. The SRE can page the on-call service owner directly from the work item, or Work Management can page the service owner automatically when specific triggers occur. As responders compare dashboards, check recent deployments, and rule out possible causes during discussion in a Slack thread, the information from Slack is automatically added to the work item’s comments. The discussion becomes part of the permanent record instead of disappearing into chat history. If the issue is serious enough, the on-call service owner can escalate the same work item to a Datadog incident . Alternatively, you can configure Work Management to automatically escalate issues that have specific attributes (for example, any P1 work item). The incident carries forward the original telemetry data and the details from Slack, so additional responders don’t need to rebuild the timeline. After responders mitigate the immediate impact, an engineering team might still need to address the root cause of the issue. Teams that work in Jira can set up Work Management to automatically create a linked Jira ticket and synchronize subsequent updates, giving engineers the investigation details along with the follow-up task. The original work item remains the common thread across the on-call page, Slack discussion, incident, Jira handoff, and final resolution. Turn feature requests into merged code Development teams can use Work Management to coordinate AI agent–driven work while keeping people involved in decisions and approvals. For example, consider a team whose feature-request backlog is growing because requests arrive faster than engineers can manually review them. When a new feature-request work item is created, Work Management can automatically assign it to a custom feature implementation agent built with Bits Agent Builder . The agent reviews the request and determines whether it has enough information to proceed. If the requirements are complete, the agent begins drafting an implementation. If details are missing, the agent tags the responsible engineer or requester in the work item to get clarification rather than guessing or silently stalling. When the requirements are clear, the agent opens a GitHub pull request (PR) and links it to the work item. The work item displays the PR status alongside the clarification history and implementation activity, giving the team one place to follow the request from intake through code review. Teams can require approval before the agent takes specific actions, so you can have a human in the loop to review and merge the code. When the PR is merged, Work Management automatically closes the linked work item so that the backlog reflects the state of the implementation without requiring manual bookkeeping. You can manage the backlog in a kanban board with saved views for different types of work items, such as bugs and feature requests. These views enable engineers to switch between workstreams without maintaining separate boards for each category. Investigate and resolve security signals in Cloud SIEM Work Management helps security teams preserve the relationship between a signal in Cloud SIEM and the investigation that the signal triggers. A high- or critical-severity signal automatically creates a security case that includes the underlying metadata and investigation details. As a result, a security analyst can begin triage immediately without having to open a case manually or gather initial context. The analyst can manage the full investigation, including ownership, status, evidence, and activity, in the same workspace where the logs, signals, and entity context exist. When the analyst is ready to act, they can trigger Datadog Workflow Automation from the security case to collect more information, notify responders, update a downstream ticket, start a remediation runbook, or run a custom Datadog AI agent. This integration moves the investigation forward without requiring the analyst to coordinate each step separately. Work Management also provides out-of-the-box analytics for the team’s broader caseload. Security leads can track unassigned security cases, mean time to assign (MTTA), and mean time to close (MTTC), giving them visibility into the health of the investigation process in addition to the outcomes of individual cases. Centralize work while preserving each team’s processes Work Management integrates with Datadog products and external systems to centralize work from across your organization. Whether a work item originates from a monitor, a Cloud SIEM signal, Slack, or another connected tool, teams can track it in one place without giving up the processes that fit their work. Each work type has its own custom attributes and statuses, so platform engineering, development, and security teams can manage different kinds of work within the same system. Work Management also meets teams at the entry points they already use. You can create and manage work items in the Work Management UI, from Slack, through Bits Chat , or from your preferred AI client by using the Datadog work items MCP toolset . Regardless of how or where a work item is created, it retains the same core fields, audit trail, and integrations. Bidirectional synchronization in Work Management keeps linked records updated across external platforms such as Jira , Linear , and ServiceNow , enabling different teams to continue working in their preferred systems. Work Management’s Slack integration sends notifications for key events, creates work items from messages, and mirrors replies from linked threads into the work item timeline. Beyond keeping work synchronized across systems, Work Management enables teams to automate what happens as work items change. Work item automation rules run when a work item is created, changes status, matches an attribute condition, or receives approvals or declines. The rules then trigger a Datadog workflow or assign a custom Datadog AI agent to perform configured actions. Together, work types, integrations, and automations enable Work Management to support distinct activities. An SRE can follow an alert into incident response, a developer can supervise an agent-generated PR, and a security analyst can investigate a Cloud SIEM signal while keeping each work item connected to the alert, request, or signal that initiated it. Start centralizing work across teams and systems with Work Management Datadog Work Management gives teams one auditable record for work performed across telemetry data, collaboration tools, external ticketing systems, automations, and Datadog AI agents. It is part of the Datadog platform at no extra cost, helping SRE, development, and security teams preserve context and ownership as work moves from detection through investigation to resolution. For more information about configuration options, read the Work Management documentation . If you don’t have a Datadog account, you can sign up for a 14-day free trial to start tracking human and AI agent–driven operational work.

title: Paying Volunteer Shuttle Drivers for Election Day Voter Transportation
summary: Why do volunteer shuttle drivers quit rides-to-the-polls programs after an election? Slow reimbursements are the culprit, same-day mileage payouts fix that gap.
body_text: Rides-to-the-polls programs run on volunteer and gig drivers, but slow reimbursement is often the reason those drivers do not come back for the next election. This piece looks at what makes volunteer driver payouts so painful, and what a faster payout process actually looks like. Every election cycle, nonprofits recruit volunteer and gig drivers to shuttle voters who cannot reach a polling place on their own, older adults, people with disabilities, and residents of neighborhoods with little or no public transit. These drivers usually front their own gas money and time, then wait for a reimbursement check that shows up weeks after Election Day, if it shows up at all. That lag matters more than it might seem. A driver who spends a Tuesday running eight or ten trips to the polls and then waits three weeks for a $60 mileage check is far less likely to sign up again next cycle. Coordinators end up re-recruiting instead of re-engaging, which is a slower and more expensive way to build a driver bench. The scale of this need is not small. Research from Tufts University's CIRCLE center found that 8% of young people without college experience cited a lack of transportation as a reason they did not vote in 2024, a barrier that fell much less on their college-educated peers. Separate research from Public Wise found that nearly 21% of nonvoters reported being kept from the polls by some kind of barrier, with limited transportation named as a recurring factor, especially in areas with fewer polling places. Transportation-based civic programs have grown in response. According to Charity Charge's roundup of nonprofit marketing programs , Lyft riders have donated more than $42 million since 2017 through round-up giving, and in 2024 alone Lyft gave over 7 million people access to discounted or donated rides supporting essentials including voting access. That kind of volume shows how much transportation-based civic infrastructure nonprofits now have to coordinate and pay for, often with a much smaller back-office team than a rideshare company. How Should Nonprofits Pay Volunteer Shuttle Drivers for Election Day Voter Transportation? Paying volunteer shuttle drivers for Election Day voter transportation usually comes down to one of two models: a per-mile reimbursement or a flat per-shift stipend. Neither model requires treating a volunteer driver as a full-time employee, but both require a way to move money quickly once a shift ends, or the program loses its best drivers within a cycle or two. Mileage-based reimbursement tends to work well for programs where trip lengths vary a lot, since it pays drivers for the actual distance covered. The IRS sets a standard rate specifically for charitable mileage each year, currently 14 cents per mile for charitable purposes in 2026, and many nonprofits use that figure, or something close to it plus a small stipend, as their baseline. Flat-rate stipends are simpler to budget and easier for drivers to understand upfront, which can help with recruitment, though they do not account for a driver who ends up covering more ground than expected. Mileage Reimbursement or Flat Stipends: What Actually Keeps Drivers Coming Back The payment model matters less than the payment speed. A driver who receives a same-day payout, whether it is calculated by mileage or a flat rate, is far more likely to volunteer again than one who is still waiting on a check three weeks later. For coordinators, this means the real design question is not mileage or stipend, but how quickly can this reach the driver's bank account or digital wallet after their last trip. Programs that can answer same day tend to see: Higher driver retention across multiple election cycles Fewer support calls asking where a payment went Less manual reconciliation for the finance or operations team running the program Do Volunteer Drivers Need to be Treated as W-2 Employees? Generally, no. Most rides-to-the-polls volunteers are paid a reimbursement or a modest stipend rather than a wage, which typically keeps them outside standard employment classification, though the exact line depends on how much control the nonprofit exercises over the driver's schedule and methods. This is one reason a flexible payments API matters. It lets a nonprofit collect the right tax forms only from the drivers who actually cross reporting thresholds, instead of forcing every volunteer through a full employee onboarding process. Is Mileage Reimbursement Taxable for Volunteer Drivers? Reimbursements that stay at or below the IRS charitable mileage rate are generally not treated as taxable income to the volunteer. If a nonprofit pays a flat stipend that runs higher than actual mileage costs, that excess can become reportable income, which is where automated 1099 tracking becomes useful for organizations paying a large volunteer pool across an election season. What Does it Cost to Automate These Payouts? This is usually where a small nonprofit hesitates, assuming automated payouts are built for companies with much bigger budgets. That is not really the case. Dots offers a starting plan around $19 a month that already includes domestic and international payouts, identity verification, and 1099 tax compliance through an API. A rides-to-the-polls program does not need the enterprise tier to get same-day payouts and automatic tax form collection for its driver pool. It needs a plan that covers the basics without a long procurement process, and that is available at a price closer to what most volunteer coordinators already have in their operations budget. A Faster, More Compliant Way to Pay Election Day Volunteers Rides-to-the-polls programs are, at their core, logistics operations run on a volunteer workforce, and that workforce responds to how well it is treated financially. Manual reimbursement, paper checks, and spreadsheet tracking might work for a handful of drivers, but they buckle quickly once a program scales to dozens of shuttle routes across a county. Legacy payout methods and general-purpose payment apps were not built for this use case. They were not designed to verify identity, collect the right tax forms, or route international-style payments to gig drivers who may not fit a standard employee profile. Dots was built specifically for this kind of contractor and volunteer payout work. It combines identity verification, automated 1099 collection , and instant payouts to a bank account or digital wallet in one API, so a coordinator is not stitching together a reimbursement form, a separate tax tool, and a bank transfer just to pay ten drivers after a Tuesday shift. For a nonprofit trying to keep its volunteer bench intact from one election to the next, that speed and compliance built into a single system is often the difference between a driver who signs up again and one who does not. If your organization is planning a voter transportation program and wants payouts that reach drivers the same day their shift ends, take a look at how Dots handles contractor and volunteer payments , and reach out to us for a demo to see whether it fits the way your team already works.

title: Best SAT Prep Options in 2026: How the Top Programs Stack Up
summary: Compare Acely, Khan Academy, Kaplan, Princeton Review, and ChatGPT on content, pricing, personalization, and score guarantees.
body_text: Quick summary Our top recommendation for SAT prep in 2026 is Acely. Traditional platforms like Kaplan and Princeton Review offer content and practice tests, but they lack real-time feedback and adaptive study plans built around a student's personal strengths and weaknesses. Acely is the best overall SAT option because it offers: The largest verified SAT practice library of any platform compared here: 30 full-length SAT practice tests and 9,000 expert-created SAT questions A personalized study plan that auto-updates after every practice session, rather than a static curriculum A purpose-built AI tutor trained on Acely's own SAT question bank, not a general-purpose chatbot A score improvement guarantee : a full refund if eligible students don't improve 200 or more points on the SAT Pricing starting at $49/month on an annual plan, with a 3-day free trial Acely is one of the strongest value platforms for SAT prep once content quality, volume and personalization are factored in. Introduction Between free tools, legacy test-prep brands, general AI chatbots, and newer adaptive platforms, choosing an SAT prep option in 2026 involves comparing very different products against each other. This article compares Acely against four of the most commonly considered alternatives for SAT prep so students and parents can compare the differences in content, pricing, and personalization side by side. The programs compared in this article are: Acely ($49–$149/month) Khan Academy (Free) Kaplan ($650+) The Princeton Review ($299–$2,199) ChatGPT (Free–$200/month) The best SAT prep options, ranked Rank Program Best For #1 Acely Students who want the most SAT content and adaptive personalization #2 Khan Academy Free foundational review and official College Board practice #3 The Princeton Review Students who want live, instructor-led classes and can afford premium pricing #4 Kaplan Families loyal to a legacy test-prep brand #5 ChatGPT Supplemental concept explanations only, not a substitute for structured prep Methodology This comparison draws on Acely's published head-to-head breakdowns against each competitor, cross-referencing SAT practice test counts, question bank size, pricing tiers, personalization features, and score guarantees. Programs were evaluated on: SAT practice content volume (tests and questions) Personalization and adaptive study planning AI tutoring quality and scope Score guarantee specificity Pricing and value Score reporting and performance tracking Free trial availability What should you look for in an SAT program? In 2026, the best SAT program will be one that is optimized for the digital SAT, is personalized and adaptive to a student's strengths and weaknesses, and increases difficulty over time to keep students consistently challenged. Look for a program that prepares you in the most optimized way, including learning Desmos and strengthening challenge areas. How do the top SAT prep options compare in 2026? Program Price SAT Tests SAT Questions Adaptive Plan AI Tutor Score Guarantee Acely $49–$149/mo 30 9,000 Yes, auto-updates Yes, test-focused 200+ pts Khan Academy Free 8 (Bluebook) ~3,500 No Khanmigo, generic ($4/mo add-on) None Kaplan $650+ 4 500 Only on $1,600+ tier $650+ tier only Higher score, unspecified Princeton Review $299–$2,199 5–9 Thousands (unspecified) Yes, structured course path Not prominently featured Select programs only ChatGPT Free–$200/mo 0 0, generated on the fly Partial, manual input Yes, generic None Acely: best overall SAT prep platform Price: $49–$149/month | Free Trial: 3 days Acely is the most complete self-paced SAT option for students who want depth of quality content and adaptive personalization. More than 50,000 students have used the platform, and it is the only one that pairs a large expert-verified SAT question bank with a study plan that updates automatically based on performance. Content volume Acely offers 30 full-length SAT practice tests and 9,000 expert-created and verified SAT questions. That is roughly 3x the SAT test volume of Khan Academy, 7x the SAT tests of Kaplan's entry tier, and more than 3x the SAT tests in Princeton Review's flagship course. ChatGPT offers zero official practice tests. Adaptive personalization Students set a goal score and test date, and Acely builds a week-by-week study plan around it. As students complete practice sessions, the plan automatically updates to reflect the areas a student should focus on to improve their score. This is a meaningful difference from Khan Academy, which has no personalized study plan, and from Kaplan, where a personalized plan is only available at the $1,600+ tier. AI tutor Acely's AI tutor is trained on Acely's own SAT question bank by its curriculum team and is restricted to SAT topics. This is different from Khan Academy's Khanmigo, a general-purpose GPT-4 tool that requires a separate paid subscription and, for students under 18, parental activation. It is also different from ChatGPT itself, which can discuss any topic, but may hallucinate and has no persistent memory of a student's performance data across sessions. Score guarantee Acely backs its SAT program with a score improvement guarantee : a full refund for eligible students who do not improve by 200 or more points. This is more specific than Kaplan's and Princeton Review's guarantees, which either don't apply broadly or don't commit to a specific point threshold. Score reporting After every practice test, students get a full score report showing what they missed, their pacing, and a direct path to similar questions, with predictions validated within plus or minus 20 points of official results. Khan Academy and ChatGPT offer no comparable reporting. Who should use Acely? Best for: Students who want the largest quality SAT content library Families who want a personalized plan and an AI tutor without paying a premium tier for it Students who've plateaued on free tools and need more structure Not ideal for: Students who specifically want live, instructor-led classes (see Princeton Review) or in-person human tutoring Learn more about how Acely works or start with SAT prep on Acely . Khan Academy: best free starting point Price: Free | Official College Board Partner Khan Academy is the default free SAT prep option in 2026, built in partnership with the College Board and integrated with Bluebook, the official digital SAT testing app. It's a strong way for students to get familiar with the digital SAT format at no cost. Where Khan Academy falls short Khan Academy has no personalized study plan (students navigate independently), no pacing insights, and no score guarantee. Its practice volume (8 tests, roughly 3,500 questions via Bluebook) is a fraction of what a paid platform like Acely provides. Khanmigo, its AI layer, is a generic assistant that costs extra and requires parental activation for minors. Who should use Khan Academy? Best for: Students on a tight budget who are building foundational skills, or as a supplement for official College Board practice material. Not ideal for: Students who've plateaued and need adaptive direction or in-depth score reporting. See the full Acely vs Khan Academy comparison. The Princeton Review: best for live instruction Price: $299 (self-paced, 5 tests) to $2,199 (flagship course) | Tutoring: $420/hour Princeton Review is a recognized legacy brand with a genuine strength: live, instructor-led classes. For students who learn best in a structured classroom setting or with one-on-one human tutoring, that's a real advantage that no self-paced platform replicates. Where the value breaks down The self-paced course at $299 includes only 5 practice tests. The flagship SAT 1400+ Course, at $2,199, includes roughly 9. Both are a small fraction of Acely's 30 SAT tests. Princeton Review doesn't prominently feature AI tutoring, and its money-back guarantee only applies to select programs. Who should use Princeton Review? Best for: Students who want live, instructor-led classes or one-on-one tutoring, and families who can absorb premium pricing for that format. Not ideal for: Budget-conscious families, or students who primarily want a large self-paced content library. See the full Acely vs Princeton Review comparison. Kaplan: legacy brand, limited content at a high price Price: $650+ (self-paced course) to $1,600+ (with personalized plan) | Tutoring: Available separately Kaplan is a long-standing name in test prep, and its "Learn It / Drill It / Prove It" framework offers a familiar structure. But its standard SAT course includes just 4 practice tests and 500 practice questions. Where the value breaks down A personalized study plan requires the $1,600+ tier, and Kaplan's AI tool, KapAdvisor, is restricted to the $650+ tier and above. There's no free trial at any tier. By comparison, Acely includes an adaptive study plan and AI tutor on every plan starting at $49/month, roughly 7x the SAT tests and 18x the SAT questions of Kaplan's entry tier. Who should use Kaplan? Best for: Families who specifically want the Kaplan name and are prepared to pay for live or higher-tier options. Not ideal for: Students who need more than a few hundred practice questions, or families comparing on a features-per-dollar basis. See the full Acely vs Kaplan comparison. ChatGPT: a general AI, not a prep platform Price: Free to $200/month ChatGPT is a capable general-purpose AI, but it wasn't built for standardized test prep. It has no official practice tests, no validated question bank, and no way to track a student's progress across sessions without manual re-entry of data each time. Where ChatGPT falls short Any SAT-style questions ChatGPT generates are created on the fly, without expert review or alignment to the actual exam's format and difficulty. It has no reliable way to score practice attempts or predict how a student would perform on test day, and it can produce incorrect math explanations or flawed reasoning, a real risk when preparing for a high-stakes exam. Who should use ChatGPT? Best for: Supplemental, low-stakes use, like a quick concept explanation or brainstorming help on the essay section, alongside a dedicated platform. Not ideal for: Primary SAT prep. Students need validated content and score tracking that ChatGPT structurally can't provide. See the full Acely vs ChatGPT comparison. What should you look for in an SAT prep platform? Score guarantee The clearest signal of a program's confidence in its own results is whether the guarantee is specific or vague. A specific guarantee, like Acely's 200-point SAT guarantee , commits to a measurable outcome. A vague "higher score" guarantee, common among legacy brands, can technically be satisfied by a one-point improvement. Content volume More practice material means more chances to build pattern recognition without memorizing answers. For students targeting a competitive score, a platform with a few hundred questions will run out of unique content quickly. Look for: At least 4 to 5 full-length practice tests, ideally more At least 1,500 to 2,000 practice questions, ideally several thousand Content quality Volume alone isn't enough. Two platforms can both advertise thousands of questions and deliver very different prep experiences depending on how that content was made and how current it is. Expert-created vs. generated on the fly. Some platforms, and general AI tools like ChatGPT, generate practice questions in real time with no expert review, no validation against official test standards, and no consistency check on format or difficulty. That introduces real risk: incorrect answers, flawed reasoning, or questions that don't resemble what a student will actually see on test day. Look for a question bank that's been written and verified by educators with subject-matter expertise, not assembled algorithmically as students go. Updated for the digital format. The SAT has moved to a digital, adaptive format, and older prep materials haven't always kept pace. Some legacy providers still reference paper-test conventions, like timing built around the discontinued SAT with Essay, in their current materials. Practice tests and content should reflect the actual digital SAT: the interface, the adaptive section structure, and the pacing conditions students will face on test day. Adaptive personalization A platform that adjusts what you study next based on how you've actually performed is more efficient than one that assigns the same content to every student regardless of their starting point. Free trial A free trial lets you evaluate fit before paying. Acely offers a 3-day free trial; Khan Academy is always free; Kaplan offers none; Princeton Review's free option is a single practice test. Final verdict: best SAT prep in 2026 Best Overall: Acely. The largest quality SAT content library, the only fully adaptive study plan among the platforms compared, a purpose-built AI tutor, and a specific score guarantee, all starting at $49/month. Best Free Option: Khan Academy. Unbeatable on price and source legitimacy for SAT foundational review. Not built for students chasing a competitive score ceiling. Best for Live Instruction: The Princeton Review. A real strength for students who want a classroom or one-on-one human tutoring experience, at a premium price. Best Legacy Brand for Families Who Want the Name: Kaplan. Recognizable, but the thinnest content library in this comparison, relative to price. Best Supplemental Tool: ChatGPT. Useful for quick explanations alongside a dedicated platform, not a replacement for one. Make sure to triple-check that the information is correct, given that ChatGPT can hallucinate. For students who want the most SAT practice content and a study plan that adapts as they improve, Acely is the clearest choice in this comparison. Still deciding? Start a free trial to explore the platform yourself.

title: Definium Therapeutics Announces Positive Topline Results from Phase 3 Voyage Study of DT120 ODT in Generalized Anxiety Disorder
summary: Study met primary and all key secondary efficacy endpoints Participants receiving DT120 ODT achieved a statistically significant reduction in…...
body_text: Definium Therapeutics Announces Positive Topline Results from Phase 3 Voyage Study of DT120 ODT in Generalized Anxiety Disorder August 12, 2026 7:00am EDT Download as PDF Study met primary and all key secondary efficacy endpoints Participants receiving DT120 ODT achieved a statistically significant reduction in Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) score, with a placebo-adjusted change of 5.4 points from baseline at Week 12 (p<0.0001, Cohen’s d=0.81) DT120 ODT was generally well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with prior clinical experience Company to host webcast today at 8:00 am EDT NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Definium Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: DFTX) ("Definium" or the "Company"), a late-stage clinical biopharmaceutical company developing a new generation of therapeutics intended to address underlying causes of psychiatric and neurological disorders, today announced positive topline results from Voyage, its first Phase 3 study of DT120 (lysergide) Orally Disintegrating Tablet (ODT) 100 µg in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). The results mark the Company’s second positive DT120 ODT Phase 3 readout, following the positive Emerge results in major depressive disorder (MDD) announced in June. Voyage met its primary endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement from baseline compared with placebo, as measured by the change in HAM-A total score at Week 12. The Least Squares (LS) mean change from baseline in HAM-A total score at Week 12 in participants who received DT120 ODT 100 µg was -11.6 compared with -6.2 for participants who received placebo, an LS mean difference of -5.4 points (p<0.0001), corresponding to a standardized effect size of d =0.81. Efficacy was rapid, with changes seen as early as Day 2 and sustained at all post-baseline timepoints in Part A. “The unprecedented efficacy demonstrated in Voyage should raise the bar for what patients and clinicians expect from GAD treatments and reinforces our belief that DT120 has the potential to redefine care for the millions of patients in need,” said Rob Barrow, Chief Executive Officer of Definium Therapeutics. “Importantly, the consistent, large effect size we’ve now observed across three studies underscores the potential of DT120 to transform psychiatry and usher in a new era of mental health care. With our Panorama topline results in GAD expected in September, we remain focused on bringing this potential new treatment to patients as quickly as possible. We are deeply grateful to the patients, investigators, site personnel, and our team whose commitment made this milestone possible.” DT120 ODT was generally well tolerated, with treatment-emergent adverse events mild to moderate in severity, transient, and predominantly occurring on the day of dosing in Part A. No new safety signals were identified, including no suicidality signal or suicidal behavior. On the day of dosing, participants were assessed hourly beginning at hour 5 post-dose on a structured end-of-session checklist (EoSC). The average time to meeting EoSC criteria was 6.4 hours for participants receiving DT120 ODT in Part A, with a median of 6.1 hours and 92% of participants meeting the EoSC criteria by hour 8. “GAD affects approximately 26 million adults in the United States, and when left untreated, can cause chronic, pervasive, and debilitating symptoms that can seriously impact a person’s daily life. It is one of the most undertreated conditions in psychiatry,” said Brian Barnett, MD, Vice Chair of Psychiatry at Cleveland Clinic, and a Voyage principal investigator. “Despite the burden of the disorder, the last new FDA-approved treatment for this condition was nearly two decades ago, and many of the patients I see have not found relief despite trying multiple therapies. A single-dose treatment option delivering meaningful benefits for 12 weeks is a promising step forward not found in today’s therapies. If approved, it could give patients and their physicians a treatment option that works through an entirely different mechanism than anything currently used in clinical practice.” Highlights from Voyage Topline Results The mean baseline HAM-A score at study entry was 28.4 in the DT120 ODT treatment group (n=107) and 27.4 in the placebo group (n=107). Primary Endpoint DT120 ODT 100 µg Placebo ODT Placebo-Adjusted Difference HAM-A: LS mean change at Week 12 -11.6 -6.2 -5.4 (p<.0001) Key Secondary Endpoints CGI-S: LS mean change at Week 12 -1.0 -0.4 -0.6 (p<.0001) HAM-A: LS mean change at Week 1 -11.9 -4.2 -7.7 (p<.0001) CGI-S: LS mean change at Day 2 -1.0 -0.2 -0.8 (p<.0001) Other Secondary Endpoints HAM-A: response rate (≥50%) at Week 12 43% 16% 27% (p<0.0001) HAM-A: remission rate (≤7) at Week 12 14% 4% 10% (p=0.0222) HAM-A: mild or better (<16) at Week 12 51% 23% 28% (p<0.0001) HAM-A = Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale; CGI-S = Clinical Global Impression-Severity Scale; LS = least squares; LS mean difference = difference in LS means of change from baseline between DT120 and placebo groups Webcast Details Definium Therapeutics management will host a webcast at 8:00 a.m. EDT today to review the Phase 3 Voyage study topline results. Listeners can register for the webcast via this link . Analysts wishing to participate in the question-and-answer session should use this link . A replay of the webcast will be available via the Investor Relations section of the Definium Therapeutics website, ir.definiumtx.com , and archived for at least 30 days after the webcast. Those who plan on participating are advised to join 15 minutes prior to the start time. About Voyage Voyage is a Phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluating the efficacy and safety of a single 100 µg dose of DT120 ODT versus placebo in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). The study consists of a 12-week double-blind period (Part A) followed by a 40-week open-label extension (Part B), during which participants may be eligible to receive up to four additional doses of DT120 ODT based on symptom severity. The study enrolled 214 participants aged 18 to 74 years across approximately 35 sites in the United States with a DSM-5-confirmed diagnosis of GAD, based on clinical assessment and the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI), and a Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) total score of at least 20 at screening and baseline. The primary endpoint is change from baseline in HAM-A total score at Week 12. Key secondary multiplicity-controlled endpoints are change from baseline in Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S) scale score at Week 12, change from baseline in HAM-A total score at Week 1, and change from baseline in CGI-S score at Day 2. Voyage is one of two pivotal Phase 3 studies in GAD. Panorama, the second Phase 3 study in GAD, is aligned with Voyage, but includes a low-dose 50 µg dose arm. Participants will be randomized 2:1:2 to receive DT120 ODT 100 µg, DT120 ODT 50 µg, or placebo. The 50 µg arm is intended to confound participants’ ability to accurately assess the dose condition to which they have been randomized. This approach continues to build on the Company’s Phase 2b study of DT120 in GAD, which the Company believes demonstrated that DT120's clinical activity is not attributable to functional unblinding and aligns with FDA guidance on the use of complementary designs across the Company’s DT120 clinical development program. The primary endpoint of Panorama is change from baseline in HAM-A total score at Week 12 between DT120 ODT 100 µg and placebo. About Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) GAD is one of the most common psychiatric disorders, affecting approximately 26 million U.S. adults.1,2 People with GAD experience constant, overwhelming worry that is hard to control. Common symptoms include fatigue, muscle tension, trouble concentrating, and difficulty sleeping.3 GAD is associated with the development of other chronic physical illnesses, as well as depression, other anxiety disorders, and trauma-related conditions. Together, these issues can seriously impact a person’s daily life, including substantial functional, economic, and quality-of-life burdens, and are associated with increased healthcare utilization and costs.4,5,6 Despite the significant personal and societal burden of GAD, there has been little innovation in the treatment of GAD in the past several decades, with the last new drug approval occurring in 2007.7 About DT120 (lysergide) Orally Disintegrating Tablet (ODT) DT120 ODT is an ergoline derivative belonging to the group of classic serotonergic psychedelics, which acts as a partial agonist at serotonin-2A (5-HT2A) receptors. DT120 ODT is Definium’s proprietary and pharmaceutically optimized formulation of LSD. DT120 ODT is an advanced formulation incorporating Catalent’s Zydis® ODT fast-dissolve technology, designed to deliver several unique advantages, including faster absorption and onset of transient cognitive, perceptual, and affective changes, improved bioavailability, and a lower incidence of gastrointestinal side effects. Definium is developing DT120 ODT, the tartrate salt form of lysergide, for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and is exploring its potential applications in other serious brain health disorders. DT120 has received Breakthrough Therapy designation from the FDA for GAD. Definium maintains a strong foundation to protect and extend the long-term value of the DT120 ODT franchise through a multi-layered intellectual property strategy spanning composition, formulation, and methods-of-use patents. About Lysergide (LSD) Lysergide (LSD) is one of the most extensively studied psychopharmaceuticals in history, with over 1,000 published reports.8 First synthesized in 1938 by Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann in his search for active principles from ergot fungus, its profound psychological effects were discovered in 1943, which transformed psychiatric research.8 LSD, a definitional classic psychedelic, temporarily alters perception, cognition, and emotion, is physiologically safe, non-addictive, and is not associated with withdrawal.8 While its precise mechanism of action in the treatment of psychiatric illness is unknown, its acute perceptual, cognitive, and affective effects are mediated by agonism of the serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A (5-HT2A) receptor, and mechanistic hypotheses suggest that it causes sustained increases in neuroplasticity in a variety of brain regions.9,10 About Definium Therapeutics The mission of Definium Therapeutics is to forge a new era of psychiatry by applying scientific rigor to psychedelics, with the goal of developing accessible treatments that unlock healing at scale. Guided by a recognition that patients deserve more than better, Definium is relentlessly advancing a new generation of therapeutics intended to address underlying causes of psychiatric and neurological disorders. By turning evidence into impact, Definium aims to change the trajectory of today’s mental health care crisis and enable a healthier future. Headquartered in New York, Definium Therapeutics trades on Nasdaq under the symbol DFTX.
